title: Crucifix
artist: Africa, Central Africa, Kongo Kingdom, Kongo-style maker(s)
medium: Copper alloy, wood, upholstery studs, and iron alloy
culture: Africa, Central Africa, Kongo Kingdom, Kongo-style maker(s)
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: René and Odette Delenne Collection, Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund
description: Made centuries after Catholicism became the Kongo Kingdom's official faith, this crucifix gives Christ braids like a Kongo man. The x-shape incised into his waist wrapper references the dikenga dia Kongo, a symbol that diagrams the life cycle's four points.

title: Primordial Chaos, No. 16 (Group I, The WU/Rose Series)
museum: Hilma af Klint Foundation, Stockholm (via Wikimedia Commons)
license: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons; artist died 1944)
description: From the first group of Hilma af Klint's Paintings for the Temple, begun in 1906. Green and gold coils spiral inward on a deep blue ground, picturing the world at its origin.

title: Morning
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund
description: Philipp Otto Runge's four-part print series Times of Day represents not only the four times of day but also the seasons and the stages of human life.

title: The First Day (Dies I): The Separation of Darkness and Light, plate 1 from "The Creation of the World"
medium: Engraving; New Holl.'s second state of two
license: Public Domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)
creditLine: Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1953
description: The first plate of Jan Muller's engraved series The Creation of the World, showing the first day, when darkness was separated from light.

title: The Seed finding Good Earth
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: L. E. Holden Fund
description: One of four prints of the biblical parable of the sower. Here the sower finds fertile soil for his seed, resulting in the bountiful harvest seen in the background.

title: Vessel in the Form of an Ostrich Egg
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust
description: Ancient Egyptian men and women loved cosmetics, and the objects that held them were given lavish treatment. Here the fanciful form is an ostrich egg.

title: Red-Figure Squat Lekythos (Oil Vessel): Birth of Erichthonios
artist: Meidias Painter (Greek, Attic, active c. 420–400 BCE)
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund
description: The earth goddess Ge (also known as Gaia) hands her baby, Erichthonios, to Athena. Erichthonios would go on to become a king of Athens.

title: The Ten Largest, No. 1, Childhood (Group IV)
medium: Tempera on paper mounted on canvas, 322 × 239 cm
museum: Hilma af Klint Foundation, Stockholm (via Wikimedia Commons)
license: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons; artist died 1944)
description: The first of The Ten Largest, Hilma af Klint's series on the stages of human life: childhood, youth, adulthood and old age. More than three meters tall, it blooms with flower-like forms on a blue ground.

title: The Ten Largest, No. 3, Youth (Group IV)
medium: Tempera on paper mounted on canvas, 321 × 240 cm
museum: Hilma af Klint Foundation, Stockholm (via Wikimedia Commons)
license: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons; artist died 1944)
description: Youth, the third panel of Hilma af Klint's The Ten Largest, a series on the stages of human life painted at monumental scale.

title: Mother and Child Figure
artist: Africa, Central Africa, Democratic Republic of Congo (most likely), Cabinda, or Republic of the Congo, probably Yombe-style maker
culture: Africa, Central Africa, Democratic Republic of Congo (most likely), Cabinda, or Republic of the Congo, probably Yombe-style maker
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund
description: Attributed to the Yombe peoples, this mother and child figure's naturalism suggests that it could have been the portrait of a real person.

title: A Poppy in Three Stages of Flowering, with a Caterpillar, Pupa and Butterfly
medium: Watercolor and gouache over traces of black chalk
license: Public Domain (The Met Open Access, CC0)
creditLine: Purchase, The Elisha Whittelsey Collection, The Elisha Whittelsey Fund, Anonymous Gift, in memory of Frits Markus, and Karen B. Cohen Fund, 2005
description: Johanna Helena Herolt, the daughter of Maria Sibylla Merian, painted a poppy in three stages of flowering together with a caterpillar, pupa and butterfly.

title: Day
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund
description: Day, from Philipp Otto Runge's Times of Day, a four-part series that also represents the seasons and the stages of human life.

title: Nautilus Cup
artist: Cornelis Jansz van der Burch (Dutch, active in Delft, d. 1615)
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
description: Nautilus shells were brought to the Netherlands from Indonesia. Skilled Dutch silversmiths mounted them in silver, creating luxurious vessels sought after by wealthy collectors.

title: The Ten Largest, No. 7, Adulthood (Group IV)
medium: Tempera on paper mounted on canvas, 315 × 235 cm
museum: Hilma af Klint Foundation, Stockholm (via Wikimedia Commons)
license: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons; artist died 1944)
description: Adulthood, the seventh panel of Hilma af Klint's The Ten Largest. Large yellow forms swell at the center, surrounded by smaller shapes and script-like lines.

title: Orchid Blossoms
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Hinman B. Hurlbut Collection
description: After three trips to Central and South America, Martin Johnson Heade made a large number of paintings of birds and flowers, especially orchids, in a tropical setting.

title: Tree Root
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Gift of various donors to the department of Asian Art (by exchange)
description: The twists and turns, ebb and flow of the natural form of the tree root can be interpreted as the energy that gives life and the endless transformations in the universe.

title: The Ten Largest, No. 10, Old Age (Group IV)
medium: Tempera on paper mounted on canvas
museum: Hilma af Klint Foundation, Stockholm (via Wikimedia Commons)
license: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons; artist died 1944)
description: The last of Hilma af Klint's The Ten Largest. In Old Age, four colored fields sit inside a calm grid on a pale pink ground.

title: Evening
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund
description: Evening, from Philipp Otto Runge's Times of Day, a four-part series that also represents the seasons and the stages of human life.

title: Low Waterfall in a Wooded Landscape with a Dead Beech Tree
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund
description: The massive silvery trunk of a dead tree juts from a dune. In Jacob van Ruisdael's landscapes, dead trees, waterfalls, and ruined buildings were visual expressions of the passage of time.

title: Sand Dunes, Carson Desert, Nevada
medium: albumen print from wet collodion negative
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: John L. Severance Fund
description: A desolate place discovered by a lonely explorer: the framing blocks the horizon and shows a single wagon, the photographer's converted portable darkroom, and only two sets of footprints.

title: Large Speos - View taken from the Sand Slope (Temple of Ramesses II), Abu Simbel
medium: salted paper print from calotype negative
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
description: Teynard sets the colossal sculptures of Abu Simbel into the context of large cliffs and vast expanses of desert. The temple was relocated in 1968 to prevent its submersion; this view no longer exists.

title: Ruins of an Ancient City
medium: oil on paper, mounted on canvas
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund
description: An imagined scene of a ruined ancient city bathed in the nostalgic glow of twilight.

title: Funerary Portrait of a Young Girl
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: John L. Severance Fund
description: Made for a burial in Roman Egypt, where mummification created a physical "duplicate" for the soul to rest in. Golden lips and jewelry may have been meant to transform the spirit, not to beautify the mortal body.

title: Male figure (nkisi nkondi)
artist: Democratic Republic of Congo or Cabinda (Angola), Kongo artist and nganga (priest)
medium: Wood, metalized glass, iron, organic material, ivory or plastic, and natural fiber
culture: Democratic Republic of Congo or Cabinda (Angola), Kongo artist and nganga (priest)
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: René and Odette Delenne Collection, Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund
description: This power figure once hosted a spirit after priests placed empowering substances inside it. When the nkisi had served its purpose, the materials were removed, stripping it of its spiritual power.

title: Burial Urn with Cover
artist: Korea, Three Kingdoms period (57 BCE–668 CE)
culture: Korea, Three Kingdoms period (57 BCE–668 CE)
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: John L. Severance Fund
description: This lidded jar once contained the cremated remains of the dead. Burial jars of this type became widespread after the introduction of Buddhism, as cremation became a common practice in Korea.

title: Bhu
artist: South India, Tamil Nadu, probably Pudokkatai, early Chola Dynasty, 10th Century
culture: South India, Tamil Nadu, probably Pudokkatai, early Chola Dynasty, 10th Century
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: John L. Severance Fund
description: One of Vishnu's two wives, Bhu, the earth goddess, holds the lotus in her left hand.

title: Night
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund
description: Night, from Philipp Otto Runge's Times of Day, a four-part series that also represents the seasons and the stages of human life.

title: Cicada
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Anonymous Gift
description: A carved jade cicada. Cicadas emerge from the earth after years underground, and in ancient Chinese art they came to be associated with rebirth.

title: Heart Scarab of Nefer
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: The Charles W. Harkness Endowment Fund
description: Amulets like the heart scarab were placed in a mummy's wrappings to protect the deceased during their journey in the afterlife. The scarab beetle was an Egyptian symbol of renewal.

title: Convolvulus and Metamorphosis of the Convolvulus Hawk Moth
medium: watercolor with touches of opaque watercolor over indications in black chalk or graphite on vellum
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: John L. Severance Fund
description: Maria Sibylla Merian reared caterpillars herself to study their life cycles. This drawing portrays the life cycle of the European pink-spotted hawk moth as well as its favorite food, the morning glory.

title: The Swan, No. 12 (Group IX/SUW)
museum: Hilma af Klint Foundation, Stockholm (via Wikimedia Commons)
license: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons; artist died 1944)
description: From Hilma af Klint's series The Swan, which explores opposites meeting and merging. A many-colored form joins a white sphere above and a brown sphere below.

title: Woman and Child
artist: Africa, Central Africa, Democratic Republic of Congo, Yombe-style carver
culture: Africa, Central Africa, Democratic Republic of Congo, Yombe-style carver
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
description: Her miter-shaped hairstyle, chiseled teeth, and raised body scars signal that the woman incarnates the founding ancestor of a kinship group.

title: Ancestor Group Portrait
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on paper
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Gift of Joyce G. Ames in honor of her husband B. Charles Ames
description: Thirty figures from various generations of ancestors, men on the right and women on the left. Scrolls of this type were displayed for worship at home during the New Year celebrations.

title: Altarpiece, No. 1 (Group X)
medium: Oil and metal leaf on canvas
museum: Hilma af Klint Foundation, Stockholm (via Wikimedia Commons)
license: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons; artist died 1944)
description: One of the three Altarpieces that close Hilma af Klint's Paintings for the Temple. A many-colored triangle rises toward a golden sun.

title: Mirror with Lotus and Mantra
license: CC0 (Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access)
creditLine: Gift of Drs. Thomas and Martha Carter in Honor of Sherman E. Lee
description: Around the central knob are four leaves, a ring of tiny beads, and a circle of small lotus flower designs; outside them, eight petal shapes each hold a Sanskrit letter.
